title: 12 Best Retail Design Agencies in 2026
summary: The 12 best retail design agencies, split into store environment firms and retail brand and packaging firms, with locations verified on each firm's own site.
body_markdown:
**Key takeaways:**


- "Retail design" means two different jobs. One builds the store; the other builds the brand you see on the shelf and the screen. This list separates them, because almost no roundup does.
- Awesomic does not design or build store interiors, and we say so plainly. We sit in the second group.
- Fit-out and packaging are different orders of magnitude: a store rollout is a construction budget, while a packaging refresh is a design one.
- If your packaging says "recyclable," FTC rules require the whole package to be recyclable and facilities to reach a substantial majority, defined as at least 60% of consumers where it sells.


Search for retail design agencies and you get two completely different kinds of company mixed together. One designs physical stores: layout, fixtures, lighting, millwork, fabrication and installation. The other designs the brand that fills them: identity, packaging, shelf presence and the digital storefront alongside.


Both are legitimately called retail design, and hiring the wrong one wastes a quarter. So this list is split into those two groups, labeled, with each firm placed where its own website says it belongs.


We are in the second group, and it is worth being direct about the limit that implies. **Awesomic does not do store environments, fixtures or fit-out.** If you need a store built, one of the five firms in the first section is your answer and we will not pretend otherwise.


What we do cover is the brand side of the shelf, which is why we keep a dedicated[retail designer](https://www.awesomic.com/hire/hire-a-retail-designer) role rather than treating retail as ordinary graphic work.


## The two things "retail design" means


A store-environment firm sells space. Its work is measured in square feet and rollouts, its deliverables are drawings, fixtures and installed millwork, and its team includes architects and often its own fabrication capacity. Engagements run in months, sometimes years, and cost what construction costs.


A retail brand and packaging firm sells what the shopper reads. Its work is identity, structural and graphic packaging, labeling, point-of-sale graphics and the e-commerce presence that now sits beside the physical shelf. Deliverables are artwork and guidelines, and the budget is a design budget.


The overlap is real but narrow. A store designer will have opinions about your brand, and a packaging designer will have opinions about your shelf. Neither substitutes for the other, and the honest question to open a call with is which of the two problems you are actually solving. If it turns out to be neither, our roundup of[graphic design agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/graphic-design-agencies) covers the broader category.

## Store environment and fit-out agencies


The five firms below design the physical store. If your project involves square footage, fixtures or a rollout, start here, and note that the top high end retail design and build agencies in this group carry fabrication in-house rather than subcontracting it.


### Chute Gerdeman


**Overview:** A retail experience design firm working on store concepts and brand environments, with a long track record in specialty retail, grocery and restaurant formats.


**Core services:**


- Store concept development from positioning through to built environment
- Environmental graphics and wayfinding inside the store
- Brand experience strategy applied to physical space


**Industries served:** Specialty retail, grocery, restaurant and food service, convenience


**Pricing:** Nothing published. Store environment work is costed per project and quoted once discovery is done.


**Pros:** genuine concept depth rather than decoration, publishes a verifiable address at 501 West Schrock Road in Westerville, Ohio, long history in the discipline


**Cons:** no published pricing, project timelines run in months, and it is far more capability than a single store needs


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes retail experience work across specialty and food retail formats.


**Why it is here:** It is the clearest example of a firm that starts with the shopper's experience rather than the floor plan.


**Final verdict:** A strong first call for a concept that has to work across many stores.


### Miller Zell


**Overview:** A brand environment firm that both designs and manufactures, describing itself as delivering environments built for scale. Its own site shows the fabrication floor rather than a studio, which tells you what it optimizes for.


**Core services:**


- Retail environment design across large store estates
- In-house fabrication of fixtures and branded elements
- Installation and rollout management across many sites


**Industries served:** National retail chains, grocery, convenience, financial services branches


**Pricing:** No rate appears online. Programs are costed by store count, then quoted.


**Pros:** design and manufacturing under one roof, built for multi-site rollouts, decades in branded environments


**Cons:** neither a rate nor a location is published, and the scale orientation suits estates rather than one boutique


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes branded environment programs for national retail and service estates.


**Where it beats the alternatives:** Controlling fabrication, which is where multi-store rollouts usually slip.


**Final verdict:** The option to consider when the problem is a hundred stores, not one.


### Sergio Mannino Studio


**Overview:** A New York studio specializing in retail interiors and brand design, working largely with specialty and design-led retailers on individually considered stores.


**Core services:**


- Retail interior design for specialty and flagship stores
- Brand design applied through the physical space
- Custom fixture and furniture design


**Industries served:** Specialty retail, fashion, home, wellness


**Pricing:** Unlisted, with interior projects costed one at a time.


**Pros:** strong design point of view, publishes a verifiable Brooklyn address at 117 Grattan Street, comfortable with smaller footprints


**Cons:** no published pricing, a smaller studio than the rollout specialists, and less suited to a national estate


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes retail interior work across specialty and consumer brands.


**Its niche:** Individual stores where the space itself has to be the brand statement.


**Final verdict:** A good fit for a flagship or a small, design-led chain.


### King Retail Solutions


**Overview:** A retail design firm covering interior design, fabrication and installation, positioned to take a store from concept through to a finished, installed environment.


**Core services:**


- Retail interior design and store planning
- Fixture fabrication for the designs it produces
- Installation, so one firm carries the project to completion


**Industries served:** Grocery, convenience, specialty retail, food service


**Pricing:** Absent from the site; work is priced per program.


**Pros:** single accountability from design through installation, practical grocery and convenience experience, avoids the design-to-build handoff


**Cons:** no published pricing, no public street address, and the integrated model gives you less freedom to shop the build separately


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes store design and build programs across food and convenience retail.


**What it is genuinely good at:** Removing the gap between the drawing and the installed fixture.


**Final verdict:** Worth a call when you want one firm answerable for the finished store.


### JPRA Architects


**Overview:** A Michigan architecture practice working across retail and mixed-use development, which puts it at the heavier end of this group where planning and permitting matter.


**Core services:**


- Retail and mixed-use architecture
- Site planning for retail developments
- Interior architecture for commercial spaces


**Industries served:** Retail developers, mixed-use, hospitality, commercial property


**Pricing:** Nothing published. Architectural work carries a per-project quote.


**Pros:** genuine architectural capability rather than interiors alone, handles the regulatory side, states Michigan as its base on its own site


**Cons:** no published pricing, architecture-led rather than brand-led, and more firm than a store refresh requires


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes retail and mixed-use development projects.


**Why it is here:** Some retail problems are building problems, and this group needs one firm that can handle those.


**Final verdict:** The right call when the project involves the building, not just the interior.

## How we chose these twelve


Two checks did most of the work, and both are things directory listings get wrong.


We read each firm's own site to decide which group it belongs in, rather than accepting the single "retail design" label that directories apply to everyone. That is the whole structure of this article, and it is the thing that saves a reader a wasted call.


We also recorded location only where a firm publishes it. Retail design has a lot of acquisitions and consolidation, and one well-known name illustrates why that matters: **CallisonRTKL** , long treated as the largest retail design practice in the world, now resolves under **Arcadis** , the engineering group that acquired it.


A roundup that copies an older list will present it as an independent firm it no longer is. Where we could not verify an address on a firm's own site, the table says "No public address" rather than guessing one. Pricing was the third check, and among the specialists it produced nothing. Not one of the eleven puts a figure on its site, so we invented no bands. The cost section below explains the shapes instead.

A store rollout is a construction budget with design attached; packaging is a design budget. Comparing them directly is the most common mistake in this category, which is why the two are separated above rather than averaged into one misleading range.


For the store side, the labor market gives a useful floor. The[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/interior-designers.htm) puts the median annual wage for interior designers at **$67,190 in May 2025** , with about **7,700 openings a year** and 3% growth projected to 2035. That is the in-house alternative, and it is why most retailers buy store design as a project rather than employing it.


The same labor market shapes the brand side. The pay and demand picture for a[graphic designer job](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/how-to-get-a-graphic-designer-job-in-u-s-companies-in-2024) explains why experienced packaging artworkers are hard to hire and harder to keep on staff.


## The packaging rule most design roundups never mention


If your packaging makes an environmental claim, it is regulated, and the design agency is not the one the regulator calls.


The FTC's Green Guides at[16 CFR Part 260](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-260) allow an unqualified "recyclable" claim only when the entire product or package, excluding minor incidental components, is recyclable, and recycling facilities are available to a **substantial majority** of consumers or communities where the item is sold. The Guides define a substantial majority as **at least 60%** .


That single rule kills a lot of well-intentioned artwork. A carton with a non-recyclable window, a pouch with a metallized liner, or a "recyclable" flash on a package sold nationally where curbside facilities are patchy all risk being deceptive.


Ask any agency you hire who is responsible for substantiating the claim, and get that answer in writing, because the Guides require every claim to be substantiated before it runs. It is one reason we brief every[packaging designer](https://www.awesomic.com/hire/hire-a-packaging-designer) on the claim as well as the artwork.


## Choosing between the two groups


Answer one question first: does this project change the space, or change the package? Space work goes to the first five firms. Package and brand work goes to the second group.


If the answer is both, sequence them rather than running them together. Brand and packaging decisions should usually land first, because a store environment designed around an identity that then changes is an expensive way to discover the order of operations.


The second question is whether the work is a project or a stream. A store concept is a project. A retail brand's packaging calendar is a stream, and it never really stops: new flavors, new sizes, new retailers with their own spec sheets, seasonal variants.


Teams carrying that load continuously usually find a subscription cheaper than repeated project scoping, and the wider set of[unlimited design services](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/best-12-unlimited-graphic-design-services-2025) shows how that market has priced it.


## FAQ


### What do retail design agencies actually do?


It depends which kind you call. Store environment firms design the physical space, covering layout, fixtures, lighting and often fabrication and installation. Retail brand design agencies handle identity, packaging, shelf graphics and the digital storefront. Both are marketed as retail design, so ask any firm to describe its last three projects before assuming which one you are talking to.


### How much do the best retail design agencies charge?


None of the eleven specialist firms in this list publishes a rate. Store work is quoted as a project or a per-store program and behaves like a construction budget, while brand and packaging work is quoted per project and behaves like a design budget. Ongoing packaging support is the one part of this category commonly available on a subscription, starting at $1,490 a month with us.


### Which are the top packaging design agencies for retail?


Among the firms here, the top packaging design agencies for retail are Turner Duckworth, SmashBrand, Design Womb and Kaleidoscope, with different strengths: global brand systems, consumer testing, food and beverage depth, and portfolio architecture respectively. Choose on category experience and whether they test, not on portfolio aesthetics alone. Craft still matters on the artwork itself, and our[print design guide](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/the-best-midjourney-prompts-for-print-design-guide) covers where generated imagery does and does not hold up in production.


### Do I need a high end retail design and build agency, or just a designer?


The top high end retail design and build agencies earn their fee when the output is a physical store, because the handoff between drawings and installed fixtures is where projects fail. Miller Zell and King Retail Solutions both fold fabrication and installation into their offer for that reason. If your output is artwork rather than millwork, a design-only firm or a subscription is the cheaper and faster route.


### Can one agency handle both store design and packaging?


Some claim to, but very few do both well, because the disciplines need different teams, and a firm strong in millwork rarely has structural packaging expertise in-house. The practical approach is to hire the specialist for the larger part of the problem and let them coordinate with the other. Sequence the brand work first so the environment gets designed around a settled identity.
